items.summary: Anaxia, the BLLM engine, with the source, the Lean development and the checks of the paper BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI by D. Bhattacharjee and U. Bhattacharya. The engine is the Python package eBLLM (command anaxia ), a Lean 4 library and the container image ghcr.io/creelie/bllm-engine, which carries no model weights. The paper proves, in a model with independent runs, that certifying self-modifications costs an entropy (the entropy law), that a sound infinite self-improvement of finite cost exists exactly when one series converges, that a proposer needs a number of proposals set by a Rényi entropy of order one half, and that n verified layers sharing one budget cost at least n log(n/θ). Sixty-five of its theorems are proved in Lean 4 with Mathlib, each depending only on the three standard axioms. The engine combines known constructions in a typed crossing network with a program check and a refuter for every candidate, a shared memory and five target agents, and builds new objects in construction mode: a goal-directed builder and an exists-forall search, each followed by an independent gate. From the rules of Steinberg's problem it rebuilds the gadgets of the 2016 counterexample of Cohen-Addad, Hebdige, Král', Li and Salgado; it finds nothing on Erdős's question for cycles of length 4 to 6. Layer towers of depth one to three, a ladder and a mesh, are compared with the crossing loop at the same number of checks. A Hodge-only run of twelve rounds leaves every target point at the same gap. None of the five benchmark problems (the lattice Yang–Mills mass gap, the Hodge conjecture, the standard conjecture of Lefschetz type, Chowla's conjecture, Erdős problem 1183) is solved. The registry of the systems, methods and collections the engine draws on, with what it takes from each and what it leaves, is src/ebllm/bllm/data/sources.json and Appendix D of the paper.
items.title: BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI

items.summary: We study unitary \(S^1\)-manifolds with four isolated fixed points in relation to Kosniowski's conjectural inequality \(4χ(M)>\dim M\). For every integer \(m\ge3\), we show that there exists a unitary \(S^1\)-manifold \(M_m^{18}\) with exactly four isolated fixed points, and these manifolds are pairwise distinct and nonzero in ordinary complex bordism. Since \(χ(M_m^{18})=4\), they give an infinite family of counterexamples to \(4χ(M)>\dim M\). By gluing two blocks formed by \(G_2/SU(3)\cong S^6\) and the unit disk $D(V)$ of 12- dimensional real $S^1$-representation $V$ along their equivariantly identified free boundaries, we explicitly construct such a manifold $M^{18}_3$. We also prove that the four-point case is null-bordant in real dimension \(16\) and in every real dimension greater than \(18\); hence \(18\) is the smallest dimension in which such a counterexample occurs.
items.title: Unitary $S^1$-Manifolds with Four Fixed Points and Kosniowski's Conjecture

items.summary: Anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate. A bounded audit of one published five-variable 2-SAT transformer separates semantic ranking, fixed-threshold fidelity, numerical effective-state geometry, agreement with the native answer, and Boolean clause-edit sufficiency. A fresh balanced bank of 4096 formulas supplies additional same-checkpoint evidence; it is not independently trained-model replication. The public package documents exact replay scope and exclusions. Some historical image-dependent checks cannot be reproduced from the public files. Native replay requires separately retrieved, hash-pinned upstream source dependencies that are not redistributed here. Short independent-training feasibility attempts did not meet the predeclared competence threshold and supply no confirmatory representation evidence. Internal AI-assisted review and producer replay are not external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. CC0 applies only to original research prose, diagrams and data. Original executable code is MIT-licensed; retained third-party components retain their own terms. Consult LICENSES.md and the dependency provenance for component-level boundaries.
items.title: Assignment-Aligned Effective States in a 2-SAT Transformer

items.summary: This reproducibility package accompanies the manuscript “Multi-Representation Stylometry of Al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya: Internal Consistency and Register Variation in Classical Arabic.” It includes the corpus metadata and frozen hashes, the Gold-V3 segmentation benchmark, segmenter validation records, normalized feature matrices, PCA materials, Eder results, robustness results, reproduction code, software and environment information, checksums, provenance records, and the publication figures. The complete transformed text of the modern edition and the full ArabicSOS production output are not included because their redistribution rights are still unresolved. Their frozen SHA-256 identifiers are provided instead. The main Eder hierarchical-clustering analyses and the matched-length Eder results can be reproduced from the matrices and code included in the package.
items.title: Reproducibility Package for "Multi-Representation Stylometry of Al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya: Internal Consistency and Register Variation in Classical Arabic"

items.summary: Devilray is a reconfigurable adversarial baseline designed to systematically explore realistic fake base station (FBS) behaviors and diagnose blind spots in existing and future detectors. Empirically anchored in the first academic analysis of a commercial FBS (C-FBS), Devilray establishes a unified four-phase pipeline and seven fundamental operational feature dimensions, systematically extending them via 3GPP specification-permitted variants. Through a modular, reconfigurable implementation, Devilray supports configuring diverse FBS instances by combining these variants across the pipeline. To govern this combinatorial operational space, Devilray incorporates a semantics-aware, rule-based dependency checker that prunes standard violations and empirically ineffective operations, defining a logically explorable space of 2,592 attack instances. Using Devilray, we evaluated seven accessible FBS detectors and surfaced adversarial blind spots rooted in assumption-bound designs. This artifact submission provides the complete Devilray source code, installation and execution guides, dependency-checker test configurations, an example FBS instance profile, all ten FBS instance profiles used in the paper, packet captures from these ten instances, and derived datasets for FBSDetector. These components support the Devilray implementation and dependency checker described in Sections 5.3 and 5.4, as well as the evaluations reported in Sections 6.1 and 8. Evaluators can install and build Devilray, execute the dependency-checker verification suite, launch Devilray using the provided configuration profiles, and rerun the FBSDetector evaluation on the included PCAP and CSV datasets. The artifact was validated on Ubuntu 22.04 and depends primarily on srsRAN 4G and LTESniffer. Executing Devilray over the air additionally requires an SDR and an isolated test environment. Also, note that conducting such experiments with UEs connected to commercial networks without appropriate safeguards may raise ethical and regulatory concerns. As described in the paper, our experiments employed a Faraday cage and repeater-based setup to prevent interference with commercial networks. Evaluators without either suitable SDR hardware or the safeguards required for over-the-air experiments can still build the complete software, exercise the dependency checker, and run the dataset-based FBSDetector evaluation. The primary goal of this artifact evaluation is to verify the availability of the source code and its basic functionality.
items.title: Devilray: A Reconfigurable Adversarial Baseline for Revealing Blind Spots in Fake Base Station Detection

items.summary: Registered protocol of a systematic review reported according to PRISMA 2020. Question: how much performance do deep-learning models for precision agriculture lose when evaluated outside their training distribution (another farm, season, region, sensor or cultivar) or deployed in real field conditions, and how is deployment evidence (latency, energy, memory, field-trial duration) reported? Status at registration: searches completed on 15-16 October 2026 (Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, OpenAlex, SpringerLink, plus citation searching); 14,174 records after deduplication; title/abstract screening not started. The protocol defines the research questions, search strategy, eligibility criteria (IN.1-IN.6, EX.1-EX.8), dual-reviewer active-learning screening with ASReview LAB and a pre-registered stopping rule (SAFE-based), the data-extraction codebook, the quality-appraisal rubric and the synthesis plan (internal-to-external relative performance loss).   Version 1.1 adds Amendment 1 (18 October 2026, before any screening decision): AI-assisted title/abstract screening with human verification.
items.title: Protocol: From benchmark to field: a systematic review of external-validation and deployment evidence for deep learning in precision agriculture

items.summary: In autonomous driving, perceiving surrounding objects is not enough: failing to understand how they move and interact over time can lead to dangerous decisions. Evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) therefore requires testing whether they connect past spatial observations to future consequences. Yet existing benchmarks often assess edge cases through basic perception questions or test temporal understanding in simple scenarios, leaving complex spatiotemporal reasoning underexplored. We introduce STRIDE (SpatioTemporal Reasoning In Driving Edge Cases), an object-centric benchmark for long-tail, safety-critical driving scenarios. STRIDE covers six task families: spatial perception, spatial understanding, temporal memory, temporal extrapolation, trajectory prediction, and scene-context awareness. It pairs multiple-choice questions probing individual spatiotemporal judgments with related free-form visual question answering (VQA) requiring detailed scene explanations and justifications of driving decisions. We prioritize scenes with unusual object behaviors and complex traffic interactions, generate reference answers from structured dataset annotations through automated procedures, and use limited language-model assistance and human verification to ensure annotation quality. Across 12 proprietary, open-weight, and driving-specialized models, even the best performer, GPT-6-Astra, achieves only 43.4% average multiple-choice accuracy, versus an approximately 20% random-choice baseline. Further analysis reveals that strong performance in describing driving scenes does not necessarily translate to accurate safety-critical judgments, and that models struggle more with reconstructing object motion than recalling past positions. STRIDE thus exposes spatiotemporal driving limitations that aggregate VQA scores can conceal.
items.title: STRIDE: Evaluating Spatiotemporal Reasoning in Driving Edge Cases

items.summary: This record holds the preregistration, code, outputs, process logs and session transcripts of a study that is also a meta-experiment on research produced almost entirely by an AI agent (Claude, model claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic, run in Claude Code) under the direction of one researcher. The substantive study asks a deliberately implausible question: is living with a cat associated with untreated dental decay among US adults? It uses public data from NHANES 2005–2006 with survey-weighted modified Poisson regression, prespecified confounders, sensitivity analyses and equivalence testing. The preregistered primary result was inconclusive (prevalence ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.36). The meta-experiment measures what producing the study took: time, human interventions, agent errors and the share of code and text written by the agent. The accompanying preprint, "Do cats rot your teeth? A by-the-book paper written by an AI agent, and what it means for scientific communication", shows how four of the 45 preregistered estimates could support a positive paper without breaking the registration, and argues that verification, not writing, is now the bottleneck of scientific communication. Version 1 (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23435708) is the frozen preregistration, deposited before any exposure–outcome association was computed and later registered on OSF (doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/RVH7J). Its files remain available in version 1. items.title: Do cats rot your teeth? Preregistration, code, outputs, process logs and transcripts of a study produced by an AI agent (NHANES 2005–2006)

items.summary: This dataset tests whether public density-functional-theory (DFT) databases can guide composition selection for metastable magnet phases. It compares energy above the convex hull and computed Fe moments from Materials Project, AFLOW, JARVIS-DFT, NOMAD (Alexandria PBE calculations), OQMD and GNoME (628 entries, snapshot 2026-10-13) with 38 published observations of phases formed in Sm–Fe and Sm–Fe–M alloys (M = Co, Ti, V, Zr, Nb, Cu, Si, Ga, Al, Mo; none found for Cr, Mn, Hf) after rapid solidification or mechanical milling, 30 of which are scored. Because no database contains the disordered TbCu7 structure, a stability proxy is built from each database's ordered parents (CaCu5, 2:17, 3:29, ThMn12); the proxy and per-family best entries are given in stability_proxy_table.csv . Main finding: Materials Project, OQMD and Alexandria place no Sm–Fe compound on the convex hull, so their energies for equilibrium Sm2Fe17, metastable TbCu7 SmFe9 and SmFe12 (not formed by melt spinning) differ by less than 5 meV/atom. JARVIS-DFT ranks them correctly but places TbCu7 SmFe9 at 89 meV/atom. AFLOW and GNoME contain no comparable entries. The package contains raw database snapshots with provenance (SHA-256), the curated observation table with DOIs, numbered pipeline scripts (Python), a QA report, four figures and documentation (codebook, limitations, verification checklist). Code: MIT. Data and documents: CC BY 4.0. AI assistance: data retrieval scripts, curation drafting and analysis code were prepared with an AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic); the author verified the numbers and decisions before release.
items.title: TbCu7 Stability Screen: validation of public DFT databases against observed metastable phases in Sm–Fe–M alloys (stability proxy table)

items.summary: Speculative decoding typically characterizes speedup by draft tokens accepted per verification round. Lossless verification preserves the target model's output distribution and thus expected completion length, making this metric a meaningful efficiency proxy. Relaxed (lossy) verification accepts tokens that lossless verification would reject, potentially altering that distribution. We identify a length inflation phenomenon: relaxed verification lengthens completions, primarily by extending reasoning traces, largely offsetting apparent gains in accepted tokens per round. We evaluate existing training-free relaxed verification rules on twelve target-drafter pairs against lossless verification on identical prompts, measuring completion length, verifier rounds, wall-clock time, and task accuracy. At each rule's most relaxed evaluated setting, relaxed verification on average accepts $1.34\times$ as many tokens per round but produces $1.54\times$ longer completions. For rules with higher acceptance lengths, tokens accepted only under relaxed verification tend to have low target-model probability, contributing to length inflation. For rules that reduce verifier rounds, accuracy typically drops substantially. Further analysis traces some failures to continued reasoning that exhausts the budget needed to deliver a final answer. Overall, accepted tokens per round alone is an unreliable measure of decoding speed under relaxed verification. Completion length and verifier rounds must also be reported to assess actual efficiency.
items.title: Acceptance Is Not Speed: Length Inflation in Training-Free Lossy Speculative Decoding

items.summary: This record accompanies the two-dimensional supplement to A gauge-invariant measure for lattice chiral fermions by Nathaniel Craig. It contains the supplement and its LaTeX source, together with the curated core reproducibility package, supplied in 65 standard tar.gz core archives and a separate evidence addendum. The supplement studies a two-dimensional chiral SU(5) theory with three conjugate-5 left-handed fermions, one 10 right-handed fermion, and five right-handed singlets. It presents an analytic measure construction on a specified admissible domain and numerical tests of selected currents, gauge responses, and determinant phases. The core archive contains all 74 scientific evidence references cited in the supplement, scientific implementations, the complete free-gap ledger, and the saved inputs needed for three principal scalar replays. It retains reports on other calculations and their limitations, but does not contain every raw matrix or intermediate record for those calculations. Extract all 65 archives into one directory to recover the complete core and run the documented checks. The remainder of the additional-data collection and the superseded full calculation archive are not included. The supported replays check saved evidence and recompute final scalar arithmetic; they do not rerun every historical current integration or matrix calculation. A separate gap replay checks the covering and residual bounds using implementation code shared with the producer. The README, result index, completeness record, manifests, and verification receipts specify the procedures and limits. These two-dimensional checks support, but do not prove, the four-dimensional result. The evidence addendum supplies 123 further scientific files referenced by the reports, including exact error ledgers, control results, fields, plots, and compact input records. Extract it alongside the 65 core archives and follow the updated README. Its verifier checks the added-file hashes and selected exact saved arithmetic for the finite-amplitude two-step curl and direct B1 endpoint comparison. It does not rerun the original matrix calculations or establish the analytic remainder estimate. License scope: Apache-2.0 for project-authored code; CC BY 4.0 for project-generated data and written documentation. Existing third-party licenses and notices remain in force. See LICENSES.txt.
items.title: Two-dimensional chiral SU(5) measure and calculation records for A gauge-invariant measure for lattice chiral fermions

items.summary: Sea level fingerprints connect the spatial distribution of rapid ice mass change to sea surface height (SSH) change, but the spatial resolving power of this inverse problem remains poorly quantified. Here we provide the first systematic, scale-resolved quantification of Greenland Ice Sheet mass change structure recoverable from its SSH fingerprint when ice loss geometry varies. We develop a physics-informed neural operator, constrained by an accurate neural-operator emulator of the forward sea level equation, to probe the information content of this ill-conditioned inverse problem. Across synthetic ice change ensembles, broad ice loss patterns can be recovered, but distinct ice fields can produce nearly identical fingerprints, so fine-scale structure depends on the assumed a-priori ice change distribution. Inversion fidelity varies with the wavelength and amplitude of ice mass change. An empirical error law separates these effects and defines a scale-dependent accuracy ceiling. For a satellite-altimetry-derived reference field, the estimated fingerprint-only ceiling is $R^2\sim0.79$ under the present SSH observation geometry and matched-prior assumption. The leading three principal components explain 99.76% of fingerprint variance, yet higher-order components retain information needed to distinguish finer ice change structure. SSH observations near Greenland carry most information on ice loss locations. Applying the leading fingerprint principal components to the observed 1993--2019 SSH rate recovers the large-scale Greenland fingerprint, while the residual field is correlated with basin-scale bathymetry, consistent with unresolved sterodynamic variability. These results establish a quantitative empirical bound on fingerprint-only ice-loss resolving power and identify how independent observations and ice sheet constraints can improve inference.
items.title: Operators Reveal Scale-Dependent Limits on Recovering Greenland Ice Loss from Sea Level Fingerprints

items.summary: Extracting generalized parton distributions (GPDs) from experimental observables, the convolution structures denoted as Compton form factors (CFFs), requires solving an intrinsic inverse problem. We presented results using NNGPD, a flexible regression method based on a physics-informed neural-network framework, for reconstructing GPDs using integral constraints -- including CFFs and Mellin moments -- and symmetry and endpoint constraints. The approach does not require pointwise training information on the underlying GPDs. Closure tests using pseudodata generated from a phenomenological model demonstrate the ability of the framework to reproduce the principal features of the underlying distributions across a range of kinematics. A Bayesian neural-network formulation is also introduced to address uncertainties associated with the reconstruction. Finally, we discussed a broader question in GPD phenomenology: whether the complete momentum-fraction dependence of GPDs is necessary to extract physical quantities such as partonic angular momentum. This motivates investigating approaches that infer Mellin moments directly from experimentally constrained CFFs, while quantifying the remaining ambiguities.
items.title: Neural Network Representation of Generalized Parton Distributions (NNGPD)

items.summary: Resampling is the standard remedy for weight degeneracy in particle filters, but in high dimensions it distorts the spectrum of the ensemble covariance in a way that is computable from the importance weights. This paper studies the inverse problem: recovering the pre-resampling spectrum from the observed weights and the empirical spectrum alone, and using it without biasing the filter. We first show that the forward spectral law extends to random importance weights once one conditions on the weights together with the realized offspring counts, rather than on the weights alone. We then construct a regularized free-deconvolution estimator, prove its consistency with an explicit error budget at a fixed resolution scale, and certify model mismatch through a computable forward residual. The repaired spectrum enters the filter only as the preconditioner of a Metropolis-adjusted rejuvenation move, so that spectral error affects mixing efficiency but not the invariant target. For the full filtering cycle, we derive a geometrically summable error recursion under stable scalar dynamics and an explicit law for the cost of abstaining from repair. Pre-registered simulations show that the inversion reduces the spectral error by an order of magnitude, that the corrected preconditioner recovers about 90% of the oracle's sampling efficiency in an anisotropic regime, and that the cost of abstention depends on when abstentions occur rather than on how many. The repair recovers eigenvalue laws, not eigenvectors, and is certified only within an explicitly stated exogenous-weight regime.
items.title: Regularized free deconvolution for spectral repair of resampling distortion in high-dimensional particle filters

items.summary: Bayesian geophysical inversion provides a probabilistic framework to estimate subsurface properties, in which uncertainties are represented by a so-called posterior probability density function (pdf). Estimating this pdf is computationally challenging when it is high dimensional or complex, particularly if it may be multimodal. We introduce Stein mixture variational inference (SMVI) for efficient Bayesian geophysical inversion with multimodal or complex posterior solutions. The method combines parametric variational inference with Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD). In SMVI, the posterior pdf is approximated by a mixture (sum) of distributions, in which component distributions are optimised jointly using the SVGD update rule. This construction combines computational efficiency with the flexibility to represent a range of plausible Earth models and allows components to be updated in parallel. Here, SMVI is first tested on two synthetic seismic inverse problems, demonstrating that SMVI can recover non-Gaussian, complex and multimodal posterior solutions accurately and efficiently. Then, we apply SMVI to real seismic data by performing Love wave tomography of the British Isles, and obtain inversion results that are consistent with previous Monte Carlo solutions. Around the East Irish Sea sedimentary basins, SMVI captures bimodal uncertainty associated with ambiguity in basin boundary locations, revealing alternative subsurface structures compatible with the observations. These results indicate that SMVI generalises various previous variational methods, and provides a practical and effective framework for quantifying complex uncertainties and supporting geological interpretation of seismic images.
items.title: Bayesian Geophysical Inversion using Stein Mixture Variational Inference for Multimodal or Complex Solutions

items.summary: Learning causal structure from data requires assumptions about mechanisms, noises, observation schemes, and interventions. Historically, causal discovery has relied primarily on conditional independence. This review focuses on modern causal discovery methods that exploit properties of distributions beyond conditional independence. Our organizing principle separates the source of identification from the statistical estimator and its computational implementation. This perspective connects conditional-independence methods with distributional asymmetries, conditional-moment restrictions, and variation across environments or individuals. We examine discovery under latent confounding and feedback, distinguishing causal information about observed variables from reconstruction of latent structure and emphasizing the additional semantics required by cyclic models. We also distinguish population identification, frequentist and Bayesian consistency, uncertainty quantification, and algorithmic guarantees. Throughout, examples show why the same observational distribution can support different conclusions under different model classes. We conclude with guidance for comparing methods at their identifiable targets and a research agenda for uncertainty, heterogeneous populations, non-scalar variables, and the intersection of discrete data, feedback, and hidden confounding.
items.title: Causal Discovery beyond Conditional Independence: Identifiability, Algorithms, and Statistical Inference for Directed Acyclic and Cyclic Graphs

items.summary: Visual counterfactual explanations (VCEs) should alter a classifier's prediction while remaining realistic and preserving decision-irrelevant content. Image-space methods provide high-quality counterfactuals but are computationally costly, whereas latent-space methods are more efficient but often less faithful. We identify two sources responsible for this gap. First, latent generation recovers a natural sample from a perturbed representation, whereas classifier guidance pushes it toward a target class, so their update directions may oppose. Second, VAE reconstruction can alter regions that should remain unchanged. We introduce CLEAR, a latent Flow Matching framework for VCEs. CLEAR uses Flow Matching's explicit instantaneous velocity as a reference for the generative direction to decompose classifier guidance into cooperative and conflicting components. It preserves the cooperative component and adaptively attenuates only the conflicting one according to conflict strength. We further analyze conflict frequency and strength throughout generation to reveal how classifier guidance interacts with the generative process. CLEAR also dynamically identifies editable regions, constrains latent modifications, and directly preserves factual content outside them to reduce VAE-induced changes. Across five bidirectional tasks on two datasets, CLEAR retains latent-space efficiency while achieving counterfactual quality comparable to or better than strong image-space baselines, with a 2.5x speedup over the strongest baseline. Project page: https://yan-zen9.github.io/CLEAR/
items.title: CLEAR: Cooperative Latent Flow for Visual Counterfactual Explanations with Accurate Region Preservation

items.summary: mm-ADL-Home is a cross-environment millimeter-wave radar point-cloud dataset for human activity recognition in furnished residential environments. The dataset was collected in four indoor environments comprising three simulated bachelor-unit layouts and one real bachelor unit, using the same activity taxonomy and radar configuration as the mm-ADL dataset (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22405011).  Each participant–environment recording is preserved as a continuous point-cloud stream and includes: (1) point_cloud.csv , containing radar point-cloud observations; (2) frame_labels.csv , containing frame-level activity annotations; (3) timestamps.csv , providing the temporal correspondence between radar and annotation frames; and (4) location_annotations.csv , containing the intervals used to register the radar sensor and landmark furniture in the radar coordinate system. The activity taxonomy covers locomotion, sitting and lying transitions, stationary sitting and lying, simulated falls, and floor-to-standing recovery. Location annotations identify sittable furniture, lieable furniture, kitchen locations, entry locations, and the radar sensor origin. These annotations support the reconstruction of room-level spatial context and furniture landmarks on the horizontal radar coordinate plane. The dataset contains complete recordings without a prescribed windowing or segmentation scheme, allowing users to implement their own preprocessing, temporal segmentation, domain adaptation, and evaluation protocols. Synchronized RGB recordings used during annotation are not included in the public release. Participant identifiers are pseudonymous.
items.title: mm-ADL-Home: A Cross-Environment Millimeter-Wave Radar Point-Cloud Dataset for Activities of Daily Living in Furnished Homes

items.summary: This working paper consolidates the mathematical correspondences studied between selected string-theory models and the Phase framework of the Harmonic Physics research programme. It presents the central equations, reported evidence and outstanding physical questions, with detailed derivations, controls and computational records retained in companion reports and reproducibility packages. A compact phase field reproduces the momentum–winding contribution of the declared circle-compactified bosonic closed-string model and preserves that contribution under reciprocal exchange of radius, momentum and winding. A quadratic optical continuation retains a reciprocal canonical description and yields a dispersion relation containing quadratic and quartic wave-number terms. A retrospective comparison with released fluid-of-light measurements favors inclusion of the retained gradient within the scope of the processed experimental records. For a specified two-component continuum action with fixed component amplitudes, constant coefficients and equal propagation speeds, the relative phase obeys an exact sine-Gordon equation, while the common phase obeys a free wave equation. This conditional classical correspondence applies at finite relative-phase excursion and connects to the equation obtained through Pohlmeyer reduction of classical bosonic strings on R_t × S². The assumptions and remaining reconstruction questions are stated explicitly. A separate conditional gravity construction maps a fixed source coefficient into a supplied Schwarzschild exterior compatible with the leading string metric condition. The construction retains explicit assumptions about spatial geometry, dimensional calibration and vacuum dynamics. The master also discusses polarization-dependent apparent position and identifies a predictive relationship between foundational Phase, observer coupling and registered distance as a continuing research question. The paper distinguishes the established mathematical correspondences and bounded optical-model evidence from the proposed foundational interpretation of Phase. Physical identification, reconstruction of the evolved breather with the required global string conditions, and quantum equivalence are not established by the reported comparisons. items.summary: Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) are flexible priors for compositional regression functions, but inference for intermediate layers faces questions. The basic obstruction is an adjacent-layer symmetry: applying an invertible transformation and its inverse to two adjacent layers leaves the composed regression map unchanged. Under explicit symmetry and prior-comparability conditions, we show that the posterior may not concentrate on any prescribed intermediate-layer representation, even when the composed regression function is estimable. We then introduce an augmented $ρ$-fractional posterior that reweights layer decompositions by a non-saturating identity-deviation penalty. The augmentation changes posterior odds between symmetry-related decompositions by an exponential penalty ratio. Under proper choices of the penalty and a prior mass condition, it preserves function-level fractional posterior contraction, while shrinking the redundant layers towards the identity mapping. Thus, the likelihood does not identify a unique ``true'' set of layers; the augmentation favors identity-biased parsimonious decompositions within an equivalence class of layers; uniqueness of a selected representative is not established.
items.title: Canonical Layer Inference for Deep Gaussian Processes via Symmetry-Breaking Augmentation

items.summary: Student-built micropositioning stages that use piezoelectric actuators are common in engineering education laboratories, yet their nanopositioning performance is routinely overstated because hysteresis in the actuator is neither characterised nor compensated. The treatment is methodological and theoretical: no observational data are reported. A Preisach-type hysteresis operator is combined with a capacitive-sensor noise model to derive closed-form expressions for the repeatability floor as a function of sweep amplitude, sensor resolution and compensation residual. First, the repeatability bound scales linearly with the uncompensated hysteresis fraction and inversely with the square root of the number of sweep segments, so that doubling sensor resolution yields only a factor-of-√2 improvement unless the compensation residual is simultaneously reduced. Second, a compensation-residual threshold exists below which further sensor refinement yields no repeatability gain; this threshold is derived explicitly. Third, the framework predicts that student-built stages operating without compensation cannot achieve sub-100 nm repeatability for sweep amplitudes above 20 V, a bound consistent with the educational literature. The contribution is a design-oriented evaluation protocol that allows instructors and students to predict repeatability limits before construction, and to allocate resources between actuator linearisation and sensor quality.
tags: piezoelectric actuator; hysteresis compensation; capacitive sensor; micropositioning stage; nanoposi
items.title: Piezoelectric-Actuator Hysteresis Compensation in Student-Built Engineering Education Micropositioning Stages: A Capacitive-Sensor Evaluation Linking Drive-Voltage Sweep to Nanopositioning Repeatability Bounds

items.summary: We study unitary \(S^1\)-manifolds with four isolated fixed points in relation to Kosniowski's conjectural inequality \(4χ(M)>\dim M\). For every integer \(m\ge3\), we show that there exists a unitary \(S^1\)-manifold \(M_m^{18}\) with exactly four isolated fixed points, and these manifolds are pairwise distinct and nonzero in ordinary complex bordism. Since \(χ(M_m^{18})=4\), they give an infinite family of counterexamples to \(4χ(M)>\dim M\). By gluing two blocks formed by \(G_2/SU(3)\cong S^6\) and the unit disk $D(V)$ of 12- dimensional real $S^1$-representation $V$ along their equivariantly identified free boundaries, we explicitly construct such a manifold $M^{18}_3$. We also prove that the four-point case is null-bordant in real dimension \(16\) and in every real dimension greater than \(18\); hence \(18\) is the smallest dimension in which such a counterexample occurs.
items.title: Unitary $S^1$-Manifolds with Four Fixed Points and Kosniowski's Conjecture

items.summary: Recent large audio language models (LALMs) have extended their capabilities beyond lexical speech understanding to tasks requiring paralinguistic and non-linguistic audio understanding, such as emotion recognition. However, these models still struggle to reliably utilize acoustic information, particularly when it co-occurs with spoken linguistic content. Existing benchmarks do not clearly distinguish acoustic perception from higher-level reasoning, making it difficult to identify the source of these failures. To address this issue, we introduce VocalGrad, a benchmark designed to evaluate LALMs' ability to perceive low-level acoustic variations. VocalGrad formulates this problem as a simple binary classification of temporal change direction, enabling evaluation largely independent of higher-level reasoning or semantic understanding. Our benchmark results reveal a substantial gap in acoustic perception between human annotators and state-of-the-art LALMs: while human annotators achieve high accuracy, LALMs perform at near-chance levels. We further conduct linear probing to identify structural bottlenecks in these models. Our analysis reveals two distinct failure modes: for some categories, task-relevant information is preserved in internal representations but not utilized by the language model head; for others, the information becomes progressively less linearly decodable across model layers. Overall, our results reveal substantial limitations of LALMs in modeling acoustic variation under controlled settings and expose representation differences not observable from text outputs.
items.title: VocalGrad: Evaluating Acoustic Perception in Audio Language Models

items.summary: Anaxia, the BLLM engine, with the source, the Lean development and the checks of the paper BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI by D. Bhattacharjee and U. Bhattacharya. The engine is the Python package eBLLM (command anaxia ), a Lean 4 library and the container image ghcr.io/creelie/bllm-engine, which carries no model weights. The paper proves, in a model with independent runs, that certifying self-modifications costs an entropy (the entropy law), that a sound infinite self-improvement of finite cost exists exactly when one series converges, that a proposer needs a number of proposals set by a Rényi entropy of order one half, and that n verified layers sharing one budget cost at least n log(n/θ). Sixty-five of its theorems are proved in Lean 4 with Mathlib, each depending only on the three standard axioms. The engine combines known constructions in a typed crossing network with a program check and a refuter for every candidate, a shared memory and five target agents, and builds new objects in construction mode: a goal-directed builder and an exists-forall search, each followed by an independent gate. From the rules of Steinberg's problem it rebuilds the gadgets of the 2016 counterexample of Cohen-Addad, Hebdige, Král', Li and Salgado; it finds nothing on Erdős's question for cycles of length 4 to 6. Layer towers of depth one to three, a ladder and a mesh, are compared with the crossing loop at the same number of checks. A Hodge-only run of twelve rounds leaves every target point at the same gap. None of the five benchmark problems (the lattice Yang–Mills mass gap, the Hodge conjecture, the standard conjecture of Lefschetz type, Chowla's conjecture, Erdős problem 1183) is solved. The registry of the systems, methods and collections the engine draws on, with what it takes from each and what it leaves, is src/ebllm/bllm/data/sources.json and Appendix D of the paper.
items.title: BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI

items.summary: LLM system capabilities depend not only on model parameters but also on the executable harnesses that organize information acquisition, tool use, reasoning, and memory. Recursive harness evolution can automate their design, but how it can reliably discover generalizable systems from limited, noisy, and repeatedly reused feedback remains unclear. We study this question in agentic video understanding, where rich multimodal evidence and coupled mechanisms make harness optimization challenging. We first introduce VHarness-BRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework that evolves video harnesses around a frozen vision-language model. Analyzing over 4,000 evolved candidates, we find it competitive with hand-engineered systems but identify three interconnected failure modes: validation overfitting, search-budget dilution, and the early-experience trap. We trace all three to a common root: the same imperfect validation evidence drives both harness revisions and the proposer's search strategy. We therefore propose VHarness-SRSI, an evidence-governed framework in which every search decision rests on evidence that is transferable, sufficient, and gathered before the search commits. It restricts the proposer to content-free feedback, informs exploration with instrumented warm-up experiments, and develops mechanisms in isolated probe-race branches before factorial composition and joint refinement. Across four video understanding benchmarks, VideoHarness-SRSI improves the equally weighted mean held-out score by 6.2% relative to VideoHarness-BRSI and reduces the mean validation-test gap by 37.9%. Reliable harness evolution thus depends on how search is organized and informed, not only on how well it optimizes validation performance.
items.title: VideoHarness-SRSI: Structured Recursive Self-Improvement for Video Understanding Harness

items.summary: Speculative decoding typically characterizes speedup by draft tokens accepted per verification round. Lossless verification preserves the target model's output distribution and thus expected completion length, making this metric a meaningful efficiency proxy. Relaxed (lossy) verification accepts tokens that lossless verification would reject, potentially altering that distribution. We identify a length inflation phenomenon: relaxed verification lengthens completions, primarily by extending reasoning traces, largely offsetting apparent gains in accepted tokens per round. We evaluate existing training-free relaxed verification rules on twelve target-drafter pairs against lossless verification on identical prompts, measuring completion length, verifier rounds, wall-clock time, and task accuracy. At each rule's most relaxed evaluated setting, relaxed verification on average accepts $1.34\times$ as many tokens per round but produces $1.54\times$ longer completions. For rules with higher acceptance lengths, tokens accepted only under relaxed verification tend to have low target-model probability, contributing to length inflation. For rules that reduce verifier rounds, accuracy typically drops substantially. Further analysis traces some failures to continued reasoning that exhausts the budget needed to deliver a final answer. Overall, accepted tokens per round alone is an unreliable measure of decoding speed under relaxed verification. Completion length and verifier rounds must also be reported to assess actual efficiency.
items.title: Acceptance Is Not Speed: Length Inflation in Training-Free Lossy Speculative Decoding

items.summary: Finite-element models, extracted results, analysis scripts and figure scripts supporting the article "Competing Failure Modes in Residually Stressed Thin Films on Flexible Substrates: Wrinkling, Channel Cracking, and Their Coupling" (International Journal of Solids and Structures). All finite-element calculations are carried out with ABAQUS/Standard 2021: the plane-strain linear-buckling benchmark and the geometrically nonlinear post-buckling sweep (imperfection, phase and mesh), the channel-crack factor and stress field, the J-integral and cohesive-zone crest-crack models, the three-dimensional stripe, checkerboard, hexagonal and herringbone wrinkle patterns, and the Al/Al2O3 equi-biaxial unit cell. The archive contains the input-generation scripts, input files, ODB post-processing scripts, results in JSON format, solver logs, the Python scripts that reproduce Figures 1–17 of the article, the figures, a README, a figure-to-source map, software versions and a SHA-256 file manifest. The three zip files unpack into one folder, thin_film_failure_modes_data.
items.title: Data and code for "Competing Failure Modes in Residually Stressed Thin Films on Flexible Substrates: Wrinkling, Channel Cracking, and Their Coupling"

items.summary: Emergency-stop circuits built by engineering technology students are routinely treated as safe once they pass a functional test at commissioning, yet the relay contact welding that dominates their failure modes is invisible to such tests and accumulates silently across the workshop's operating life. The framework represents a student-built circuit as a series safety function whose integrity is degraded by contact welding, and derives the conditions under which a welded contact converts a demanded stop into an undetected loss of safety function. A replication-based evaluation of the before-after-control-impact estimator was conducted under a declared variance structure with a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0, a residual standard deviation of 4.5 and an intraclass correlation of 0.64, across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The evaluation indicates that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power, and that the minimum detectable effect at 80% power falls as the number of clusters rises. The framework proposes that workshop safety assurance should shift from commissioning-time functional testing to integrity monitoring that is sensitive to contact welding, and the design analysis implies that cluster-level evaluations of such interventions require cluster counts well above those typical of single-institution studies.
tags: emergency-stop circuits; functional safety; relay contact welding; fault injection; injury-risk expo
items.title: Functional-Safety-Integrity Degradation of Student-Built Emergency-Stop Circuits in Engineering Technology Education Workshops: A Fault-Injection Evaluation Linking Relay Contact Welding to Operator Injury-Risk Exposure

Four independent faults: the plugin never followed the v29 evidence_section_NN.json rename, looped sections 02..13 , read argument_groups.*.supporting_findings cite-key strings as finding records, and swallowed every read failure in catch { continue } . Nothing depends on this repository programmatically, and reviews already produced carry their own copy of skills/ , so they are unaffected.

items.summary: Myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA) and ischaemia with non-obstructive coronary artery disease (INOCA) are increasingly recognised syndromes in which endothelial dysfunction forms the mechanistic bridge between vascular biology and clinical ischaemia. In health, the endothelium preserves vascular homeostasis by regulating tone, platelet activity, and inflammation; when this regulation fails, vessels assume a pro-constrictive, pro-thrombotic, and pro-inflammatory state capable of causing epicardial vasospasm, microvascular dysfunction, or plaque erosion—provoking genuine infarction and arrhythmias despite unobstructed arteries. This paper follows the continuum from these mechanisms to their clinical expression. It traces the evolution from early angiographic observations to contemporary imaging such as CMR, IVUS, and OCT, and outlines a chronological diagnostic pathway from the emergency department to the catheterisation laboratory. Subtle but actionable clues are highlighted across the clinical history, ECG, echocardiography, and angiography, demonstrating that a positive, mechanism-based diagnosis of endothelial dysfunction is feasible even when invasive testing is unavailable. Management is directed by the dominant mechanism calcium-channel blockers and nitrates for vasospastic angina; β-blockers or metabolic agents for microvascular angina supported by endothelial stabilisers, cardiac rehabilitation, and psychosocial care. Persistent endothelial dysfunction is associated with later heart-failure development, particularly HFpEF, emphasising the need     for   early   recognition     and     tailored   therapy.   The  chapter concludes with real-world challenges and emerging perspectives, including standardised testing, AI-assisted imaging, and precision therapeutics. Ultimately, understanding endothelial dysfunction links mechanisms to clinical practice, reframing MINOCA and INOCA as diagnosable and treatable syndromes that demand mechanism-based, preventive care.
tags: Endothelial dysfunction; MINOCA; INOCA; Coronary microvascular dysfunction; Vasospastic angina; Hear
items.title: Endothelial Dysfunction in Myocardial Infarction With Non-Obstructive Coronary Arteries and Ischemia With Non-Obstructive Coronary Arteries: Mechanisms and Clinical Approach

items.summary: Which biological findings enter a reported explanation depends on how the model population was constructed, a choice predictive validation alone does not reveal. We fitted 10,000 L2-regularised logistic regression models to TCGA pan-cancer tumour-versus-normal data: 100 regularisation strengths on 100 train-test splits, with patients fixed within each split. Strongly and weakly regularised models differ in mean accuracy by only 0.21 percentage points, yet prioritise different genes systematically with regularisation strength. Averaging explanations across a hyperparameter grid produces a top-50 panel sharing 41 genes with a single fitted model, but which model depends on the grid centre (Spearman correlation 0.92, 350 simulated practitioners). For 43 of 50 practitioners, the panel combines genes from strongly and weakly regularised models more fully than any fitted model: the explanation belongs to no model whose accuracy was established. A conventional grid recovers only a quarter of genes favoured exclusively by the strongest regularisation. HMGCS2 ranks among the top 50 in 73 of 100 strongly regularised fits and no weakly regularised fits, yet appears in none of 50 simulated reports. Reconstructing a published biomarker workflow on 20 cohort resamples reveals a different failure: the closest refit contains only 23 of the averaged panel's 50 genes, and no panel gene appears in all 20 refits. We define model-relative provenance as how much of a panel any single fitted model contains, distinct from workflow provenance recording how an analysis was run. We provide measurements to make the model population, the choice that selects from it, and that provenance reportable.
items.title: Same Accuracy, Different Gene Panels: How the Hyperparameter Grid Chooses the Reported Explanation

items.summary: Diffusion-based multimodal large language models (dMLLMs) decode by iterative denoising with bidirectional attention, which precludes the standard autoregressive key--value cache. Practical deployments therefore rely on approximate caching that reuses intermediate states across denoising steps. Such caching, however, often makes a response repeat one token at adjacent positions in a run that breaks the sentence, a failure we term the \emph{Repeat Curse}. Tracing the context-token information flow reveals three disruptions. Within a step, caching disperses the attention that anchors a position on nearby context tokens. Across steps, similarity-based refresh is not staleness-aware, so some positions are decoded against stale key--value states. Across layers, the deep-layer entropy of the context fails to converge where repetition arises. We accordingly propose CoTA++, a training-free, plug-and-play framework that counteracts each disruption where it originates: Context-Token Attention Re-anchoring re-forms the attention routing against the current context, Decode-Aware Refresh reserves part of the cache's refresh budget for the positions about to be committed, and Context-Token Entropy-Guided Voting discounts the confidence of a position by the deep-layer entropy of its context, which reorders the unmasking. The three components act at non-overlapping stages of a decoding step and compose freely with existing dMLLMs and caches. Across three dMLLMs and two caching backends, CoTA++ reduces the sample repetition rate of long responses from up to 99.6\% to at most 17.0\%, recovers most of the accuracy lost to caching on nine benchmarks, and keeps the speedup of caching at under 15\% overhead, making approximate caching reliable for dMLLMs.
items.title: CoTA++: Understanding the Repeat Curse in dMLLMs from an Information Flow Perspective

items.summary: This dataset contains longitudinal field observations of group size and composition and localized climate metrics for a wild population of cooperatively breeding apostlebirds ( Struthidea cinerea). Data were collected over five consecutive breeding seasons (2006–2010) at Fowlers Gap Arid Zone Research Station in New South Wales, Australia. The primary objective of this dataset was to evaluate two competing hypotheses regarding the adaptive value of cooperative group living under environmental variability: the 'social buffering hypothesis' whereby helpers mitigate unfavourable environmental conditions (e.g. drought or extreme heat) to reduce the likelihood of reproductive failure; and the 'social capitalisation hypothesis' whereby helpers enhance reproductive output under favourable climatic conditions.
items.title: Dataset for: Fair-weather friends: Group size boosts reproduction in wet and cooler conditions, in a dryland cooperative breeder

items.summary: Oscilloscope probe compensation kits circulate between teaching laboratories, yet the calibration status of a kit is rarely transferred with the same rigour as the instrument it serves. the present analysis treats cross-course calibration transfer as a metrological problem and evaluates, by round-robin design, how bandwidth attenuation in a probe kit propagates into measurement discrepancy bounds when the kit is moved between courses. The evaluation is a replication-based characterisation of the before-after-control-impact estimator under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64), with power estimated across 2000 design cells at cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points.54 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power, and that the minimum detectable effect falls steeply as cluster count rises from 8 to 32. A first-order attenuation model links probe bandwidth to the fractional amplitude error at the test frequency, and the round-robin design is shown to bound the transfer discrepancy that a receiving course can expect. The contribution is a design-level calibration-transfer protocol that makes the discrepancy bound explicit before a kit leaves its home course, rather than after a student records a suspect waveform.
tags: probe compensation; calibration transfer; round-robin evaluation; bandwidth attenuation; measurement
items.title: Cross-Course Calibration Transfer of Oscilloscope Probe Compensation Kits in Engineering Education: A Round-Robin Evaluation Linking Bandwidth Attenuation to Measurement Discrepancy Bounds

items.summary: This working paper consolidates the mathematical correspondences studied between selected string-theory models and the Phase framework of the Harmonic Physics research programme. It presents the central equations, reported evidence and outstanding physical questions, with detailed derivations, controls and computational records retained in companion reports and reproducibility packages. A compact phase field reproduces the momentum–winding contribution of the declared circle-compactified bosonic closed-string model and preserves that contribution under reciprocal exchange of radius, momentum and winding. A quadratic optical continuation retains a reciprocal canonical description and yields a dispersion relation containing quadratic and quartic wave-number terms. A retrospective comparison with released fluid-of-light measurements favors inclusion of the retained gradient within the scope of the processed experimental records. For a specified two-component continuum action with fixed component amplitudes, constant coefficients and equal propagation speeds, the relative phase obeys an exact sine-Gordon equation, while the common phase obeys a free wave equation. This conditional classical correspondence applies at finite relative-phase excursion and connects to the equation obtained through Pohlmeyer reduction of classical bosonic strings on R_t × S². The assumptions and remaining reconstruction questions are stated explicitly. A separate conditional gravity construction maps a fixed source coefficient into a supplied Schwarzschild exterior compatible with the leading string metric condition. The construction retains explicit assumptions about spatial geometry, dimensional calibration and vacuum dynamics. The master also discusses polarization-dependent apparent position and identifies a predictive relationship between foundational Phase, observer coupling and registered distance as a continuing research question. The paper distinguishes the established mathematical correspondences and bounded optical-model evidence from the proposed foundational interpretation of Phase. Physical identification, reconstruction of the evolved breather with the required global string conditions, and quantum equivalence are not established by the reported comparisons. Future substantive revisions will be released as new numbered Zenodo versions, accompanied by a dated summary of changes. Please cite the specific version consulted. Detailed methods, results and reproducibility materials are documented in the companion publication, Giant Magnon Amplitude and Phase Correspondences : https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23463422 . items.summary: In autonomous driving, perceiving surrounding objects is not enough: failing to understand how they move and interact over time can lead to dangerous decisions. Evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) therefore requires testing whether they connect past spatial observations to future consequences. Yet existing benchmarks often assess edge cases through basic perception questions or test temporal understanding in simple scenarios, leaving complex spatiotemporal reasoning underexplored. We introduce STRIDE (SpatioTemporal Reasoning In Driving Edge Cases), an object-centric benchmark for long-tail, safety-critical driving scenarios. STRIDE covers six task families: spatial perception, spatial understanding, temporal memory, temporal extrapolation, trajectory prediction, and scene-context awareness. It pairs multiple-choice questions probing individual spatiotemporal judgments with related free-form visual question answering (VQA) requiring detailed scene explanations and justifications of driving decisions. We prioritize scenes with unusual object behaviors and complex traffic interactions, generate reference answers from structured dataset annotations through automated procedures, and use limited language-model assistance and human verification to ensure annotation quality. Across 12 proprietary, open-weight, and driving-specialized models, even the best performer, GPT-6-Astra, achieves only 43.4% average multiple-choice accuracy, versus an approximately 20% random-choice baseline. Further analysis reveals that strong performance in describing driving scenes does not necessarily translate to accurate safety-critical judgments, and that models struggle more with reconstructing object motion than recalling past positions. STRIDE thus exposes spatiotemporal driving limitations that aggregate VQA scores can conceal.
items.title: STRIDE: Evaluating Spatiotemporal Reasoning in Driving Edge Cases

items.summary: Student-built load banks used in undergraduate electrical machines laboratories typically derive rotor speed from a slotted-disc tachometer whose pulse train is quantised by a fixed sampling clock, and the resulting slip estimate feeds directly into the torque-speed curve that students report. the present analysis treats the slip estimator as a formal object and derives its sampling distribution under a declared measurement model in which the tachometer quantisation interval is the dominant error source. The slip estimator is biased, that the bias is a function of the ratio of quantisation interval to synchronous period, and that the bias propagates into the torque-speed curve as a systematic displacement of the pull-out region rather than as random scatter. A replication-based evaluation was conducted: 600 data sets of N = 500 were drawn from a declared data-generating process (intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35, error SD 4.2), and the ordinary least squares estimator was characterised under the stated process. The estimated bias for the intercept was -0.02315 and for the exposure coefficient 0.00064; the root mean squared errors were 0.88484 and 0.01581 respectively; empirical coverage of the nominal 95% confidence intervals was 1.0 for both parameters. The results indicate that the estimator is essentially unbiased for the slope but that the intercept carries a small negative displacement, and that the quantisation mechanism identified analytically is consistent with the direction and magnitude of the observed intercept bias. The stroboscopic benchmark should be reported alongside the torque-speed curve so that the slip bias is visible to the student and to the assessor.
tags: induction motor; slip estimation; tachometer quantisation; torque-speed curve; engineering education
items.title: Induction-Motor Slip Estimation Bias in Student-Built Engineering Education Load Banks: A Stroboscopic Speed Benchmark Linking Tachometer Quantization to Torque-Speed Curve Reliability

items.summary: This computational package accompanies the Neuro-Symbolic MAPE-K governance testbed for agentic retrieval-augmented generation at the edge. It provides Python source, experimental inputs, measured outputs, provenance manifests, analysis tables, figures and readable evidence reports for two related campaigns: the October 2026 MAPE-K controller campaign and the separate 18 October 2026 dense-retriever control campaign. The retriever control records 3,744 retrieval trials and 640 clean-validation query evaluations across sparse, pretrained dense and clean-fitted dense retrievers. It performs no new generator or controller evaluation. The package preserves campaign-specific directory layouts and historical execution records. A dependency-light deterministic template smoke test supports inspection without language-model downloads or CUDA. Full inference and fitting used NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX 8 GB and platform-specific CUDA/PyTorch environments. Original host paths and observed package inventories are provenance records, not a universal portable lockfile; full main-campaign model weights are referenced by revision and checksum, while the retriever campaign includes its pretrained and clean-fitted checkpoints. A release verifier checks the curated file manifest and metadata. The original retrieval verifier also requires original source paths for its final host-specific integrity checks. Original project software is MIT licensed (SPDX: MIT), with collective copyright held by the MAPE-K contributors. Third-party terms remain applicable: O*NET 31.0 and UCI Adult-derived data and fixtures are CC BY 4.0 with attribution and modification notices; MiniLM model material and its clean-fitted derivative are Apache-2.0; BGE model material and its clean-fitted derivative are MIT with upstream attribution. File-specific notices, exact model revisions and checksums are retained. Experimental counts reuse base profiles and should not be interpreted as independent efficacy replications. The evidence does not establish population fairness, human-validated answer-quality superiority, or a guarantee of safe retrieved evidence.
items.title: Neuro-Symbolic MAPE-K: Computational Package and Retriever Control

items.summary: Space Semiconductor Fabrication and Starship Nanofoundries at the Limit English Description and Research Position This research monograph asks which semiconductor unit processes could achieve a defensible mission advantage in microgravity, vacuum, radiation, remote-operation, and closed-resource environments. It does not assume that a complete advanced fab can operate in space. Instead, it compares crystal growth, deposition, etching, lithography, metrology, bonding, packaging, repair, and recycling against ground manufacture plus transport, launched spares, on-orbit packaging, and local repair. Every claimed advantage must survive matched controls, full functional qualification, and explicit mass, energy, heat, crew, contamination, maintenance, waste, and return ledgers. The volume contains 82 chapters with five research sections per chapter, 30 linked formula derivations, 200 detailed Research Gates, DOI-anchored references, and a formula-chapter-experiment-Gate crosswalk. Its central contribution is a mission-scale evidence architecture that connects process physics to contained workcells, independent metrology, safe autonomy, repair, return, circular resources, cross-platform reproduction, and successor reconstruction. Safety and irreversible environmental harm operate as hard vetoes rather than compensable score components. The literature base includes peer-reviewed DOI sources on microgravity semiconductor growth, in-space manufacturing, additive nanomanufacturing, atomic-layer processing, radiation effects, lunar resource extraction, digital twins, autonomous laboratories, and reproducible science. Recent orbital results are treated as early evidence for specific mechanisms, not as confirmation of a complete space foundry. Core research question Under what physical and mission conditions can a semiconductor unit process performed in space outperform ground manufacture plus transport or a narrower in-space alternative while preserving safety, resource closure, qualification, and independent reconstruction? Research architecture • Space-specific process advantage and strongest comparator • Environmental physics and bounded process window • Closed mass energy heat contamination and evidence ledgers • Autonomy safeing repair return and independent qualification • Cross-platform reproduction successor rebuild and retirement Recommended citation note This is an exploratory research architecture. Candidate equations are measurement and mission-decision instruments, not universal laws. Empirical use requires process-specific units, preregistration, matched controls, aerospace and semiconductor expertise, independent qualification, and cross-platform replication.

items.summary: PHOTONIC CRYSTAL MICROROBOTICS AT THE LIMIT FLAGSHIP 12/30 | STARLI INSTITUTE XXIV | GROUP B This prospective research monograph examines whether bandgap engineering and localized photonic crystal modes can enable physically predictable, reversible optical manipulation of microscopic agents when actual device geometry, absorption, hydrodynamic flow, surface adhesion, thermal limits, and task cost are fully considered. The three core couplings are photonic bands, microstructure response, and controllable motion. The book separates optical modes from attributable electromagnetic momentum transfer, and further separates externally steered particles or cells from autonomous microrobots. Its falsifiable research design compares two lattice-defect geometries, source-frequency interventions, local thermal controls, optimized free-space optical tweezers, non-periodic waveguide traps, and blinded second-chip replication. High Q or strong local field alone is not accepted as evidence of useful lower-power microrobotic performance. The manuscript contains 778 pages, approximately 119,409 English words in chapter openings and substantive chapter-body pages, 30 mathematical derivation signposts with mapped chapters and research questions, 82 research chapters, 410 individually paginated scientific study units, 200 detailed Research Gates, and 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos. An external DOI evidence ledger clarifies which physical contexts are supported by published work; four existing STARLI monographs supply intellectual genealogy, not experimental corroboration. An Excel research atlas offers equation-chapter-Gate-DOI navigation. A research Gate poses a future experiment, not a completed trial. Each door may be falsified, reinterpreted, or developed into a more testable hypothesis. The project prioritizes measurable physical mechanism, credible classical comparators, complete power and loss accounting, reproducible material controls, and release/recovery of agents. Negative outcomes are intentionally preserved as routes for later human and AI research successors.

items.summary: Emergency-stop circuits built by engineering technology students are routinely treated as safe once they pass a functional test at commissioning, yet the relay contact welding that dominates their failure modes is invisible to such tests and accumulates silently across the workshop's operating life. The framework represents a student-built circuit as a series safety function whose integrity is degraded by contact welding, and derives the conditions under which a welded contact converts a demanded stop into an undetected loss of safety function. A replication-based evaluation of the before-after-control-impact estimator was conducted under a declared variance structure with a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0, a residual standard deviation of 4.5 and an intraclass correlation of 0.64, across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The evaluation indicates that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power, and that the minimum detectable effect at 80% power falls as the number of clusters rises. The framework proposes that workshop safety assurance should shift from commissioning-time functional testing to integrity monitoring that is sensitive to contact welding, and the design analysis implies that cluster-level evaluations of such interventions require cluster counts well above those typical of single-institution studies.
tags: emergency-stop circuits; functional safety; relay contact welding; fault injection; injury-risk expo
items.title: Functional-Safety-Integrity Degradation of Student-Built Emergency-Stop Circuits in Engineering Technology Education Workshops: A Fault-Injection Evaluation Linking Relay Contact Welding to Operator Injury-Risk Exposure

items.summary: Reproducible and analytically robust research findings are essential to scientific progress, but evaluating these properties typically requires costly manual effort. We investigate whether LLM agents can help automate reproduction and robustness analysis, using a medical case study grounded in the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database, a widely used U.S. cancer registry underlying tens of thousands of published studies. First, we introduce SEER-Repro, a benchmark of 20 published SEER-based papers together with the data and resources required to reproduce their findings. Second, we create an AI agent that successfully reproduces 77.4% of 2,190 atomic claims, while providing executable baselines for further analysis. Third, we develop an agentic analysis pipeline to test the robustness of the medical findings by identifying analytical choices underlying each finding, proposing defensible alternatives, and rerunning the analysis to determine whether those choices affect the conclusion. Across published papers in SEER-Repro, our pipeline identifies potentially consequential analytical choices in 9.5% of fully reproduced findings and flags them for expert review. These results show how LLM agents can support scientific review by reproducing findings, systematically testing their robustness, and directing expert attention toward potentially consequential analytical choices.
items.title: AI-Driven Reproducibility and Analytical Robustness in Scientific Discovery
